titulo: Inequality: is the gap between rich and poor still widening?

fuente.nota: Written for the language panel. The figures are approximate and should not be cited as a source.

parrafos: Few economic questions provoke as much passion as inequality. Politicians on the left warn that the rich are pulling away from everyone else; those on the right reply that living standards for the poor have never been higher. Both may be partly right, because the answer depends on what is measured, where and over which period. A careful look at the evidence reveals a picture that is more complicated, and more interesting, than either side usually admits.

Start with the global view. For most of the twentieth century, the gap between rich and poor countries grew wider. Since around 1990, however, the trend has reversed. Rapid growth in China, India and other parts of Asia has lifted hundreds of millions of people out of extreme poverty and allowed incomes in poorer nations to catch up. As a result, most economists agree that inequality among all the world’s citizens, taken together, has fallen over the past three decades, although progress slowed during the pandemic.

Inside countries, the story is different. In many rich economies, the share of national income going to the top has risen considerably since the 1980s. The change has been most dramatic in the United States, where the richest tenth of the population now receives close to half of all pre-tax income, according to widely cited studies. In Britain, inequality jumped in the 1980s and has remained broadly stable since then. Continental Europe has seen smaller increases, and in some countries almost none at all.

Several forces help to explain this divergence. Technology has rewarded workers with advanced skills while automating many routine jobs in factories and offices. Globalisation has put low-skilled workers in rich countries in competition with cheaper labour abroad. Trade unions have lost members and bargaining power. And tax systems have generally become less progressive, with lower top rates on income and capital. Economists still debate the relative weight of each factor, but few doubt that all of them have played a part.

Wealth is far more unequally distributed than income. In most developed countries, the richest tenth of households owns more than half of all assets, while the poorer half owns only a small fraction. The rise in house prices and stock markets over the past two decades, helped by very low interest rates, has benefited those who already owned property and shares. Young people, in particular, have found it increasingly difficult to buy a home, which has become one of the main sources of frustration in countries such as Spain.

It is important, however, to distinguish between inequality before and after the state intervenes. Taxes and social transfers, such as pensions, unemployment benefits and family allowances, reduce income gaps substantially in Europe. In some countries the reduction is so large that inequality of disposable income has barely changed for decades, even as inequality of market income has increased. The welfare state, in other words, is doing a great deal of quiet work, and debates that ignore it give a misleading impression.

Recent years have also brought some surprises. After the pandemic, labour markets in many countries became very tight, and wages at the bottom rose faster than those at the top. Increases in the minimum wage, including significant ones in Spain and Germany, contributed to this narrowing. At the same time, high inflation hit poorer households harder, because they spend a larger share of their income on food and energy. The overall effect varied from country to country, but it was not the simple widening that many had predicted.

Measurement itself is a source of controversy. Surveys and tax records can give contrasting results, and the very top of the distribution is notoriously hard to observe, since the wealthiest often hold assets through complex structures or abroad. Some researchers argue that the rise of the top one per cent has been exaggerated; others believe it has been underestimated. These technical disputes matter, because they shape policy proposals such as taxes on large fortunes.

Why should inequality concern us at all, if the poor are better off than before? Economists offer several reasons. Very high inequality may reduce social mobility, as children from wealthy families enjoy better education and more useful connections. It may weaken demand, since the rich save a larger share of their income. And it can damage trust in institutions and feed political polarisation, as many voters come to feel that the system is rigged against them. Others point out that some inequality is the natural result of rewarding effort, risk and innovation, and that what matters most is whether everyone has a fair chance to get ahead.

What can governments do? The menu of options is long, and every item on it is contested. Some economists favour higher taxes on top incomes, inheritances or large fortunes; others warn that capital is mobile and that such taxes raise little money while encouraging the rich to move elsewhere. Many agree, however, that investment in early education, training and affordable housing can reduce inequality of opportunity without damaging growth. Closing the loopholes that allow multinational companies and wealthy individuals to shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions is another area where international cooperation, including within the European Union, has made some progress in recent years.

So is the gap still widening? The honest answer is that it depends. Globally, it has narrowed. In the United States, it has widened sharply, although the trend seems to have paused recently. In much of Europe, income inequality after taxes and transfers has been relatively stable, while wealth inequality and access to housing have become more pressing concerns. For policymakers, the lesson is that there is no single trend to fight, but several distinct problems, each of which requires its own response.
titulo_es: Inequality: is the gap between rich and poor still widening?
resumen_es: An analysis of how inequality has evolved: lower on a global scale, higher within many rich countries, with nuances about wealth, the welfare state and measurement problems.

ideas_clave.idea: Whether inequality is rising depends on what is measured, where and when, so both sides of the political debate are partly right.
At world level, inequality has declined since about 1990 thanks to fast growth in Asian emerging economies.
Within many rich countries, especially the US, top incomes have gained ground since the 1980s because of technology, globalisation, weaker unions and less progressive taxes.
Wealth is even more concentrated than income, and rising asset prices have made home ownership harder for young people.
In Europe, taxes and benefits greatly reduce income gaps, so disposable-income inequality has been fairly stable.
After the pandemic, tight labour markets and higher minimum wages narrowed pay gaps, although inflation hurt the poor more.
Data limitations, especially at the very top, fuel disagreement about the scale of the problem and about wealth taxes.
Inequality matters because it can reduce mobility and demand and fuel polarisation, although some degree of it rewards effort and innovation.
Policy responses range from taxing top incomes and wealth, which is disputed, to broadly accepted investment in education and housing and international action against tax avoidance.
There is no single trend but several separate problems that call for specific policies.

resumen_modelo: The article examines whether the gap between rich and poor is still growing and argues that the answer depends on the measure, the country and the period considered. At the global level, inequality has decreased since around 1990, mainly because rapid growth in Asia has reduced extreme poverty and allowed poorer countries to catch up. Within many advanced economies, by contrast, the share of income captured by the richest has grown since the 1980s, most strikingly in the United States, whereas the increase has been more modest in continental Europe. Technological change, globalisation, the decline of trade unions and less progressive taxation are cited as the main causes. Wealth is even more concentrated than income, and soaring property and share prices have made it difficult for young people to buy housing. However, in Europe, taxes and social benefits significantly reduce these gaps, keeping inequality of disposable income fairly stable. After the pandemic, low-paid workers saw their wages rise faster, partly thanks to minimum-wage increases, although inflation affected them more severely. Measurement problems also explain why experts disagree. The author also notes that inequality can harm mobility, demand and trust in institutions, and reviews possible responses, from contested wealth taxes to investment in education and housing. He concludes that policymakers face several distinct problems rather than a single trend.

preguntas.pregunta: Why has global inequality fallen since around 1990?
opciones: Because rich countries have stopped growing
Because of rapid growth in China, India and other Asian countries
respuestas: Because of rapid growth in China, India and other Asian countries
preguntas.cita: Rapid growth in China, India and other parts of Asia has lifted hundreds of millions of people out of extreme poverty
preguntas.explicacion: The text attributes the fall to rapid growth in Asia. It does not say that rich countries stopped growing or mention aid; the pandemic, on the contrary, slowed progress.

preguntas.explicacion: In the United Kingdom inequality rose in the 1980s and has remained stable since; it has not continued to increase.

preguntas.pregunta: What does the author mean when he says that the welfare state ‘is doing a great deal of quiet work’?
respuestas: He means that taxes and social benefits significantly reduce the inequality created by the market, often without people noticing. As a result, disposable-income inequality in some European countries has hardly changed even though market inequality has grown.
preguntas.cita: The welfare state, in other words, is doing a great deal of quiet work
preguntas.explicacion: The expression highlights the redistributive effect of taxes and benefits, which is not very visible but is important.

preguntas.cita: The honest answer is that it depends.
preguntas.explicacion: The conclusion qualifies the question in the title and distinguishes between the global level, the United States and Europe.
